How MachineSlotLotChange table is used: 
1. Run start: scan every loaded slot. Insert one change row per slot, all pointing at the first BarcodeBuild in that run (sequence 1 by insert).
2. Reel/lot swap: insert one row for that MachineSlotId, with BarcodeBuildId = the next board that will run (the occupancy applies from that unit onward).
3. What is on board X: BOM slots for this build’s BOM. Among changes in this BuildId whose BarcodeBuildId is <= X’s BarcodeBuildId, take the latest row per MachineSlotId.
4. Current machine map: same query against the latest BarcodeBuild in the run.
5. Which part of the batch had lot L in slot S: from that change’s BarcodeBuildId until the next change on the same slot (or end of run).
Reason why we use a composite pk is to enforce uniqueness (only one row for each component-attribute join) as a byproduct instead of an additional UNIQUE constraint

We can add the ComponentTypeId field to ComponentAttribute if we want to enforce, on a DB level, the attributes of a specific component type only being applied to the correct component. Instead of the app level (which I think is more reasonable, only fields a user sees are the ones associated with the component type)
For something like 20.0k, would we want to have some smart conversion fields? Like 20,000, ohm, conversion via k...?

We will use varchar(100) and convert on app level, or use computed valuedecimal column should we need to sort via number values. This is already done elsewhere on other app(s), so shouldn't really be a problem. We can limit it to lower varchar if we wish.

We will need to recreate NonBarcodedInfo as this new non barcoded row table, we can keep same name. We surely shouldn't use integer to store the rows, I would imagine bigint is the safest and not to worry about it
